stories.title: [Name Only Title] Dawson Knox
stories.summary:
After signing a hefty contract, he is by far having his worst year as a pro. I really thought the 3 headed TE trio of Kincaid/Knox/Hawes would be a serious weapon going forward especially with Moore being out. It has been anything, but that so far. Kincaid had a strong start, but he’s slowed down considerably. I’m guessing he’s dealing w/ some nagging injury.
	 



	I love me some Knox and he has had some massive catches and TD celebrations over the years, but I was not a fan of shelling out that much money in the offseason for a backup TE. Especially with the emergence of Jackson Hawes last year. 20 million is too much if you’re just paying a guy to block. Maybe Allen nudged management to retain him, who knows? Knox has been here for 9 years and the Bills tend to take care of longer tenured players.  He will be 30 in November so age also could be playing a part in his decline. 
	 



	Knox is on pace for his worst statistical season with less than 100 total receiving yards total and 1/3 of the season already in the books. I really hope they can get him more involved because he is an above average TE when healthy. Especially in the playoffs when guys are all beat up.

stories.title: Colten Chaos Dazzles as Sabres blank Sharks, 2-0
stories.summary:
Score: Buffalo Sabres 2, San Jose Sharks 0



Shots: Buffalo 40 – 23 San Jose 



Buffalo Sabres Goals: Zellweger (3) (Helenius, Power); Benson (1) (Thompson, Power)



San Jose Sharks Goals: N/A



Summary



In spite of a lofty shot total and a bevy of scoring chances, the Buffalo Sabres blanked the San Jose Sharks by a score of 2-0 on Tuesday night. Colten Ellis was the story of the game, stopping 24 shots for his second career shutout and the team’s first of the season. Olen Zellweger gave the Sabres the 1-0 lead early in the second, and Zach Benson gave them the insurance marker with an empty netter in the final minute of the game.



High Octane First



The game got off to a sloppy, low pace start as the game saw a few stoppages early on, including Louis Crevier flipping the puck over the glass to give the Sharks a power play just 1:30 into the period. The Sharks, however, would give that penalty right back as Josh Norris found himself on a breakaway, drawing a slashing penalty to go back to 4-4 hockey. 




JOSH NORRIS?!?!?!?! pic.twitter.com/0s5mxJeYSG— Crossing Swords ⚔️ (@CrossSwordsPod) October 28, 2026




Macklin Celebrini made his presence felt early, generating high quality chances that the Sharks were unable to convert, including picking Rasmus Dahlin’s pocket a couple times. Celebrini got the best of the Sabres’ captain a couple times early, though nothing found its way past Colten Ellis. 




Rasmus????? pic.twitter.com/lqiPrYrMqL— Crossing Swords ⚔️ (@CrossSwordsPod) October 28, 2026




Then the Sabres got cooking a bit, thanks to the line of Norris, Ryan McLeod, and Jason Zucker. That group got several nice opportunities on Yaraslov Askarov, including Zucker trying to bank it in off the Sharks’ goalie. The defensemen for the Sabres got involved as well, as Dahlin and Mattias Samuelsson found themselves on a 2-1, with Dahlin feeding a pass to Samuelsson that was shot just wide.



Those two continued to create chances, as Dahlin dangled around old friend Michael Kesselring, bringing the puck to the wall and finding Samuelsson in the slot, generating yet another quality chance that Askarov had to stop. 




Dahlin used the booty to throw a reverse check on Gaudette #LetsGoBuffalo #SJSharks pic.twitter.com/TcCd2Bj5XY— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 28, 2026




The Sabres continued to dictate pace, getting many good looks but were unable to finish, which is a growing trend for the team this season. The Sharks would get another look on the power play, however, as Crevier found himself in the box again, this time on a questionable call fighting for position by the net. The Sharks were able to get several good looks on the man advantage, highlighted by Ellis having to make a huge blocker save on a shot wide open in the slot to keep the game scoreless in the waning minutes of the first period. 



The revamped lines for the Sabres were all firing in the first, as with a few minutes left, Konsta Helenius and Tage Thompson combined for an excellent chance, as Dahlin and Helenius played pitch and catch at the blue line, leading to Helenius taking the puck behind the net finding a wide open Thompson between the circles. Askarov made the save and dove for the rebound, but every Sabres line generated something strong in the first period. The lines have been one of the biggest stories 11 games into the season, as they have changed in effectively every game so far this season, but this first period probably featured the best hockey the forward group has collectively played all season. 




Ellis save on Gaudette #LetsGoBuffalo #SJSharks pic.twitter.com/avTLfrMN9t— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 28, 2026




The Sharks wouldn’t stay quiet for long though, as we got a classic “Colten Chaos” sequence with the Sabres goaltender making several high leverage saves as the Celebrini line got to work again in the Sabres zone. The Sabres withstood another late flurry, with Celebrini getting another golden opportunity that Ellis was able to stop, this time from the left circle.




Östlund stops this one from going in pic.twitter.com/1ReGQVSRpX— Crossing Swords ⚔️ (@CrossSwordsPod) October 28, 2026




The period ended 0-0, but not for lack of trying. The Sabres outshot the Sharks 16-12, and 28 combined shots is the most in an NHL period this season to result in no goals. The Sabres held an xG edge of 1.39-1.26 after the first period. 



Second Period Chaos



The Sabres translated that high energy first period into early success in the second. Just 50 seconds into the period, Helenius found Olen Zellweger on an odd man rush, and Zellweger ripped a shot through Askarov to give the Sabres a 1-0 lead. It was Zellweger’s third goal of the season, and a nice impression for Helenius getting to play between Thompson and Zach Benson. Owen Power picked up the second assist, as he started the breakout from the defensive zone. 




Olen Zellweger, 1-0 #LetsGoBuffalo #SJSharks pic.twitter.com/AGPuKBa6CD— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 28, 2026




If not for Askarov, however, the Sabres would have found themselves a couple goals up. The Sharks were struggling to generate much of anything for the first half of the second period, while the Sabres remained all over. McLeod found Zucker for a shot in the slot that Askarov kept out, while the rebound bounced out to Crevier, who was robbed by a scrambling Askarov to keep it 1-0 with 13 minutes left in the second. 



The Sharks did finally generate a sequence of glorious chances, once again kept out on a Colten Chaos sequence. A shot made its way past Ellis off the stick of Michael Misa, but it hit old friend Michael Kesselring in the shin and deflected wide, leading to a full on scramble drill where Ellis was able to find the puck and cover it. 




Chaos around the Sabres net! #LetsGoBuffalo #SJSharks pic.twitter.com/Fb8Th9RPrh— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 28, 2026




Ellis made another tremendous save mere moments later, robbing a cross ice pass from Celebrini to Colin Graf with the left pad to keep it 1-0. Helenius also blocked a shot off the rebound, once again providing Ellis some help to maintain the lead. 




Ellis save on Graf 👀#LetsGoBuffalo #SJSharks pic.twitter.com/maaYG4ptVZ— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 28, 2026




With eight minutes left, the Sabres found themselves with their first real power play opportunity on the night as Dahlin took a high stick. Zach Benson still remains one of the most snake bitten players in the league, as on that power play, he had a redirection off a Dahlin shot stopped, then had a glorious chance right in front of the net that did not find its way in. The Sabres, though unable to convert, did put up a pretty good showing on the man advantage, though we are wearing thin on power play moral victories.



The Sabres continued to dominate possession and shot attempts for effectively the rest of the period, but the Sharks did find themselves with a late power play, as Benson went to the box for holding with 21 seconds remaining in the second period. The Sharks held possession for that full 21 seconds, but thanks to a huge shot block by Josh Norris, were unable to get anything on Ellis. The Sabres actually were able to hold a lead heading into the third period, by that same score of 1-0. They held an edge in shots on goal 30-17, and held the xG edge, 2.41-2.09. 




WHAT A WAY TO LAY OUT THE BODIES TO KEEP IT SCORELESS THROUGH TWO pic.twitter.com/LM4blerioM— Crossing Swords ⚔️ (@CrossSwordsPod) October 28, 2026




Stout Third Period



The Sharks did start the third period with a pretty lengthy power play opportunity after the penalty late in the second period, though the Sabres penalty kill was once again stout, not allowing the Sharks to get too much with the man advantage. 



With 17:11 remaining in the game, the Sabres would get another power play opportunity of their own, as Thompson came soaring up the wing, too quickly for Adam Gaudette to handle cleanly, being forced to hold him to prevent a greater chance. While the firs extended power play for the Sabres featured several chances, the second one was more of the same old Sabres, being largely ineffective and unable to set up. 




The beautiful game (and ugly Sabres power play) pic.twitter.com/TwCwVOeMjZ— Crossing Swords ⚔️ (@CrossSwordsPod) October 28, 2026




Immediately after the man advantage expired for the Sabres, the Sharks once again found themselves with a flurry of glroius scoring chances but once again Ellis was somehow able to keep them all out of the net, even losing his stick on this sequence. 



The Sharks made repeated pushes to try and break through, but the Sabres defense held pretty firm, not allowing much in the way of Ellis in the middle part of the period, and what did get to Ellis was knocked down. The line of Zucker-Norris-McLeod combined for their best chance of the third period, requiring an excellent pad save by Askarov to make a save on Zucker on a cross-ice feed from Norris. 



Ellis was tested again with four minutes left, as a shot from Kesselring took a bad bounce off the glass and popped right back out in front to Kiefer Sherwood, who was all alone in front of Ellis, but he whiffed on the shot and stuck it right into Ellis, holding the score at 1-0 still in the dying minutes. 




Ellis save on Sherwood #LetsGoBuffalo #SJSharks pic.twitter.com/GjrpNOrdZL— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 28, 2026




Askarov was then tasked with keeping the deficit at one, and he once again delivered, denying Noah Ostlund on a cross ice one timer with just 2:30 left in the game. 



The Sabres fended off an empty net push from the Sharks, keeping everything outside, until Tage Thompson flipped a puck out to center ice where Zach Benson went to work. He took Ivar Stenburg to the wall, turned him around, outmuscled him to the puck and got it to open in front, and with a heroic lunge, poked it into the empty net for his first goal of the season, securing a win for the Sabres. This was the team’s 40th shot of the contest. 




Stenberg wasn't prepared for Zach Benson. 2-0 ENG #LetsGoBuffalo #SJSharks pic.twitter.com/QFYsOAGGF4— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 28, 2026




Ellis secured the Sabres’ first shutout of the season, stopping all 24 Sharks shots, including some highlight reel saves. This was the second career shutout for Ellis. 



Wrap Up



The Sabres had an interesting reversal of a trend that has plagued them all season, as three of the four forward lines were quite impactful, while the Doan-Ostlund-Quinn line was the one that wasn’t quite holding up their end of the bargain. It is probably not a coincidence that line struggled without Benson, and Thompson and Helenius were really good with Benson.



There will defintely be a question of what to do in net for the Sabres, as you have to imagine Ellis gets the next start. He was tremendous for the Sabres on Tuesday night (Wednesday morning?), giving the team by far the best performance they’ve had in net this season. 



Much has been made of Ryan McLeod’s struggles to start the season, and while he did not record a point in this game, his performance took a huge leap playing next to Jason Zucker, who have made an excellent duo for their entire tenure in blue and gold. Those two, along with Norris, were the Sabres three leaders in xG% in the victory against the Sharks. 



In only their third opportunity of the season to hold a lead in the third period, the Sabres did an excellent job. The Sharks had just seven shots in the third period, and mustered 0.7 xG in the period despite trailing the entire time. The team simply kept their foot on the gas and were rewarded for their efforts. 



What’s Next



The Sabres remain on the west coast, as they will take on the Anaheim Ducks on Thursday night at 10 p.m.

stories.title: Game #12 Preview & Open Thread: Sabres at Sharks
stories.summary:
Buffalo begins its California swing, looking to turn overtime points into wins



Buffalo Sabres (4-4-3) at San Jose Sharks (6-5-1)



Puck Drop: 10:30 p.m. ET | SAP Center, San Jose, CATV: ESPN | Streaming: ESPN+Radio: WGR 550 / Buffalo Sabres App



The Buffalo Sabres have become very good at getting games to overtime. Now they need to start winning more of them. Buffalo begins the California portion of its four-game road trip tonight against the San Jose Sharks. Four of Buffalo’s last five games have gone to overtime, and four of the Sabers’ five road games this season have gone beyond regulation. They enter tonight 4-4-3 overall and 1-1-3 on the road. The Sabres have shown they can respond. Now they have to show they can control a game before they put themselves in a position where a comeback is necessary.



Know Your Opponent



San Jose Sharks



Record: 6-5-1 | 13 PTSLast Game: 6-4 loss at BostonDivision Ranking: 4th, PacificPower Play: 26.8%Penalty Kill: 80.5%Season Series: First meeting



San Jose has quietly become one of the more interesting young teams in the Western Conference. The Sharks return home after a 3-2-1 road trip. Their final game was a 6-4 loss in Boston, where San Jose carried a 3-2 lead into the third period before the Bruins scored four times. That result also showed the two different sides of the Sharks. They can score. They can also give up a lot. San Jose has scored around three goals per game, but it has already allowed 43 goals through 12 games. The Sharks have surrendered 139 high-danger scoring chances and have blown two-goal leads four different times this season. Plenty of talent here, though, and almost all of the conversation starts with one player.



Macklin Celebrini.



The 20-year-old captain enters tonight with five goals and 15 points, averaging 22:42 of ice time per game. That workload is among the highest in the NHL for any forward. This isn’t the rebuilding Sharks team Buffalo was accustomed to seeing a few years ago. They are young, fast, and dangerous.



What to Watch



1. Can Buffalo Play Its Third Period Game for 60 Minutes?



Josh Doan probably summed up Buffalo’s season better than anyone after Saturday’s loss. The Sabres have repeatedly found another level when games reach the third period. The problem is what happens before then. Buffalo has spent too much of the season chasing games or trying to repair damage from bad stretches. Saturday was slightly different: the Sabres actually built a 2-0 lead, only to watch Washington score three times in the second period. Buffalo then turned up the pressure in the third and eventually forced overtime. The ability to come back is encouraging. Constantly needing to do it isn’t. San Jose is exactly the kind of opponent Buffalo should attack early. The Sharks surrender chances and have struggled to protect leads. If the Sabres can establish their forecheck, force turnovers, and get traffic around the net, there should be opportunities. But giving Celebrini and the Sharks confidence early is asking for trouble. Buffalo needs to make its best hockey the standard, not the emergency response.



2. Dealing With Macklin Celebrini



No. 71 may be the most important assignment tonight. Celebrini leads San Jose in goals and points and has quickly become the engine of the Sharks’ offense. He is also dangerous in just about every way possible. Celebrini can carry the puck through the neutral zone. He can create off the rush. He can distribute. He can finish. And San Jose isn’t afraid to leave him on the ice. He enters tonight with 15 points in 12 games, and NHL.com notes he could become the first Sharks player since 2013-14 to start a season with points in each of his first five home games. The matchup puts even more responsibility on Buffalo’s top defensive pair of Rasmus Dahlin and Mattias Samuelsson. But this can’t just be about those two. Buffalo’s forwards need to make Celebrini defend. Don’t turn pucks over through the middle. Don’t allow San Jose to attack with numbers. And definitely don’t give one of the NHL’s more dangerous young stars repeated power-play opportunities. Make him spend some time playing without the puck.



3. The Special Teams Gap Is Getting Hard to Ignore



This might be the biggest statistical mismatch tonight. San Jose’s power play has converted on roughly 27 percent of its opportunities. Buffalo’s power play is sitting at just over 10 percent. That is a substantial difference. The Sabres have enough offensive talent for the power play to be better than this. Tage Thompson, Jack Quinn, Zach Benson, Noah Östlund and Rasmus Dahlin give Buffalo a unit with shooting ability, puck movement and creativity. At some point, the results have to catch up. The problem isn’t limited to the power play, either. Buffalo’s penalty kill has also struggled early in the season, while San Jose has already shown that its special teams can change games. The Sharks scored twice on the power play and once shorthanded in Saturday’s loss to Boston. San Jose also leads the NHL with four shorthanded goals. That should get Buffalo’s attention. This is not the night for careless offensive-zone penalties or lazy passes at the blue line. A relatively even 5-on-5 game could quickly tilt toward San Jose if Buffalo keeps losing the special-teams battle.



4. Jack Quinn Is Starting to Look Dangerous



While parts of Buffalo’s offense have struggled to find consistency, Jack Quinn is heating up. Quinn enters tonight on a four-game point streak, with three goals and four assists in that stretch. And he likes playing San Jose. Quinn has nine points in eight career games against the Sharks, including his first NHL hat trick and a four-point performance against San Jose last March. Lindy Ruff has Quinn skating with Noah Östlund and Josh Doan tonight. That line could be important. Östlund provides the playmaking. Doan brings a direct, hard-working presence. Quinn adds a shooter who can turn one clean opportunity into a goal. With Buffalo searching for more consistent offense, Quinn becoming a legitimate scoring threat every night would go a long way.

Injured: Alexander Wennberg, Igor Chernyshov



Luca Cagnoni is expected to return to San Jose’s lineup after sitting out the previous three games.



One More Thing: Overtime, Anyone?



Maybe don’t make early plans for the end of this one. Buffalo has gone beyond regulation in four of its last five games. Four of its five road games have gone to overtime. San Jose isn’t much different. Five of the Sharks’ six victories have come in overtime or a shootout, and they are 5-1 in games that have gone beyond regulation. So if this game is tied late in the third period, nobody should be particularly surprised. Buffalo would probably prefer not to find out. A West Coast start time could end in the early hours on the East Coast.



Final Thoughts



This is a sneaky important game for the Sabres. Not because Game 12 is a must-win, but because Buffalo needs to turn stretches of good hockey into actual wins. A 4-4-3 record isn’t disastrous. Eleven points through 11 games keeps Buffalo within striking distance. But constantly digging out of holes, struggling on special teams, and settling for overtime points isn’t a formula the Sabres want to rely on for six months. Every team in the Atlantic Division is at a 0.500 record or better, and the Sabres do not want to fall behind.



San Jose presents an interesting test. The Sharks have more talent than in years. Celebrini can take over a game. Their power play is dangerous. Their young forwards can skate. They also give up chances, have struggled to hold leads, and are coming off a game in which they surrendered four third-period goals. Buffalo has won seven of its last eight meetings with San Jose, outscoring the Sharks 35-18, and has won four straight games at SAP Center. There is an opportunity here. Get the Thompson line going. Let Quinn continue his hot streak. Stay out of the box. Make Celebrini work for everything. And maybe, for once, don’t wait until the third period to play your best hockey.

stories.title: Capitals Tuch In the Sleepwalking Sabres, Beat Buffalo 4-3 in OT
stories.summary:
Former Sabre and Dylan Strome Doom the Blue and Gold



Score: Buffalo Sabres 3-4 Washington CapitalsShots: BUF 21-34 WASH



Buffalo Sabres Goals: Quinn 6th (Zellweger, Benson) Doan 2nd (McLeod) Östlund 3rd (Power, Dahlin)Washington Capitals Goals: Tuch 6th (Kyrou) Strome 2nd (Kyrou, Chychrun) Strome 3rd (Sourdif, Fehérváry) Tuch 7th (Strome, Chychrun)



Plus 1: Making them Count



Buffalo had some good chances early but struggled to get pucks on net. Jack Quinn showed them the way. After some sustained pressure and a nice dish from Olen Zellweger, Quinn drove to the net and fired a shot from close range, beating goaltender Charlie Lindgren. It was the Sabres’ first shot on goal, and Quinn continues to pile up the points. Zach Benson picked up his seventh assist of the season on the play as well. It was a big opening goal on the road for the boys in Blue and Gold.



Sabres starter Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen made a few nice stops after the goal as Washington began turning up the pressure. Buffalo eventually cleared the zone and worked the puck down ice, where a brutal turnover by the Capitals’ defense handed the Sabres a 2-0 lead. Jakob Chychrun’s drop pass to nobody was intercepted, as Ryan McLeod stole it along the boards. He quickly spun and passed the puck to Josh Doan who wasted no time firing it on net. Lindgren got a piece of it but the puck deflected by him and into the net. It was a gift-wrapped tally that the struggling Doan was more than happy to accept, giving him just his second goal of the season.



Then, the inevitable happened. Under pressure deep in their own zone, Sabres defenseman Dennis Gilbert (in for Zach Metsa) had his pass blocked, leaving the puck bouncing around in a dangerous area. Former Sabre Alex Tuch eventually came up with it and swept the puck toward the net, where Tage Thompson perfectly tipped it past Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen to cut Buffalo’s lead in half. If you were a betting man, you just cashed in on that one happening.



The Capitals generated a few more shots to close out the period and held an 8-5 advantage in shots on goal after 20 minutes. Buffalo’s speed was on full display for much of the opening frame, but it didn’t translate into many shots. At least the Sabres made the most of their limited opportunities, taking a 2-1 lead into the first intermission.







Minus 1: Second Period Sleepwalking



Mattias Samuelsson took the game’s first penalty, getting called for slashing Washington’s Tom Wilson. Buffalo’s beleaguered penalty kill did a solid job keeping the Capitals at bay with some strong defensive coverage. However, the Sabres couldn’t finish the job. Just after the penalty expired, Jakob Chychrun kept a clearing attempt in at the blue line and fired the puck toward the net. Dylan Strome had slipped behind the defense and swept home the rebound past Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen before the goaltender could fully extend his pad.



Just like that, the game was tied, and the momentum had swung firmly in favor of the home team.



It took some time, but Buffalo finally started generating chances again, using its speed and skill to put pressure on Washington. Jack Quinn had the best opportunity, only to be denied by Lindgren. Luukkonen came up with several strong saves of his own as the game began to open up, with play becoming much more evenly contested.



Washington’s physicality began to take hold late in the period, seemingly wearing down the Sabres a bit. Olen Zellweger then inadvertently sent the puck over the glass while attempting to clear the zone, handing the Capitals yet another power play. Once again, Buffalo would have to rely on its struggling penalty kill to keep Washington off the scoreboard. Spolier alert: They did. But once again the Caps would capitalize soon after, with Strome cashing in for his second of the game. Buffalo’s defensive coverage wasn’t tight enough, and a quick shot off a pass from the corner somehow eluded Buffalo’s goalie. Luukkonen appeared to be in good position, but the puck still managed to slip through. 



A clutch save WAS made just before the period ended, as Lingren came up large for Washington. The Caps scored three straight goals, and once again, the Sabres have yet to hold a lead after two periods in a single game this season. Buffalo simply stopped skating with the same urgency and intensity they showed in the first period, allowing the Capitals to take control of the game.



Minus 2: Tuch and Roll Over in OT



Buffalo started the third period with some good pressure, and came close twice with two shots off the crossbar. The Sabres continued adding to their already enormous total of pucks hitting iron this season.



Lindy Ruff’s team would keep up the pressure as the Sabres second line would come to the rescue again, along with a little luck. Noah Östlund was credited with a ping-pong goal off a Captial player’s leg that casually slid right into the net. That trio was buzzing again but it was the defense who picked up the apples on the play, with Power and Dahlin collecting the assists.



Buffalo would then get two consecutive power plays looking to take the lead but failed to capitalize on either, even with Alex Tuch in the penalty box for the second one. The ineptitude of the man advantage continues to kill this team, as two glorious opportunities go to waste again.



Things got feisty as Dennis Gilbert cleared out a few Capitals players from around the crease after Luukkonen made a strong save amid a scramble in front of the net. No penalties were called, but the face-washing was plentiful as tempers began to flare.



Konsta Helenius would take a careless high sticking call with six minutes to go and Buffalo would be tested one last time.They pulled it off, and didn’t allow a goal soon after either. Both teams played it back and forth until the horn went and the Sabres scratched and clawed the game to overtime, a familiar regularity for this team lately.



If you’ve read this far, you already know things went exactly as scripted by the hockey gods—and that aforementioned betting man. After some decent early Buffalo pressure, Alex Tuch was fed the puck from Strome behind the net right in the slot and scored his second of the game and the OT winner. It looked like Luukkonen may have been screened on the play but to quote the legendary Bob Uecker, “To hell with it!” I shut it off and didn’t see the replay.



This is all part of the plan, you see. The Universe will stop at nothing to make us suffer. Meanwhile, Buffalo picks up a point (woopity-doo!) and remains stuck at two regulation wins while going nowhere fast.



Final Thoughts:



The Sabres let this game slip away achingly and Dylan Strome was dominant. Up by two goals and giving up three straight before eeking out the OT and falling in dramatic but expected fashion. Did Tuch shoot WIDE this game? I didn’t see it if he did.



Tage Thompson (and the whole top line) along with Rasmus Dahlin were non factors for most of this game. Not what you want to see from your top players. Zach Benson, Noah Östlund and Jack Quinn once again carried the load.



The start of Buffalo’s California road trip begins on Tuesday night, October 27th at the San Jose Sharks. The game starts at 10:30 pm Buffalo time. Sabres After Dark will be worth the watch with San Jose’s young star Macklin Celebrini showcasing his skills.

What to watch



A familiar face



For the first time since his departure from the Sabres this offseason, Alex Tuch will face his former team.



Tuch, who signed an 8-year, $10.5 million AAV contract with Washington in a sign-and-trade, has had a solid start to the season, scoring five goals, including one shorthanded, to go with two assists. He is second on Washington in points, one behind Ryan Leonard.



By all accounts, Tuch was a well-respected figure in Buffalo’s locker room, and it’s hard to imagine there will be too much animosity toward the 30-year-old from his former teammates — though there will surely be some chirps. That said, the best way to show Tuch the grass isn’t always greener would be with a win.



Sabres riding with Luukkonen



At long last, our international nightmare is over: the Connor Hellebuyck trade saga is no more, and we can finally give the Heritage Classic its proper respect.



Jokes aside, the Jets traded the three-time Vezina Trophy winner to New Jersey on Friday for four players and two draft picks, ending months of rumors and the hopes of many Sabres fans, as Buffalo had long been reported to be interested in Hellebuyck. Instead, the Sabres will continue to roll with Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen and Colten Ellis, who have combined for -5.2 goals saved above expected this season per Hockeystats.com, while Alex Lyon remains on injured reserve.



Luukkonen, who was in the center of trade conversations surrounding Hellebuyck, told reporters Friday, “I think it’s good for everybody that some of that noise quiets down.” The 27-year-old will surely hope that the noise surrounding his poor start to the season will be silenced next.



Good power play spot?



The Sabres power play has been far from powerful this season, but the matchup against the Capitals could present some opportunities to shift the narrative. 



Washington’s penalty kill has allowed 8.7 expected goals against per 60 this season, good for 27th in the NHL according to Hockeystats.com, while the Sabres’ last five opponents all rank in the top half of the league in that category.



With Buffalo coming off a power play goal against Philadelphia, as well as another man advantage that yielded a handful of chances but no goal, it could be a good spot to continue building some momentum in a part of the Sabres’ game that could really use it.



Injury Notes

Glaring Issues Highlight Buffalo’s Disappointing Start
stories.summary:
Sabres Struggling in Several Areas and it is Costing Them



The Buffalo Sabres are off to an underwhelming 4-4-2 start to the season, and the fans are growing increasingly restless. Recurring structural flaws continue to plague this team, and after ten games, Buffalo has held a lead heading into the third period exactly ZERO times. While that speaks to the Sabres’ ability to battle back and claw their way into games, it’s hardly a sustainable way to operate over an 84-game season.



The problems are piling up, and what might have been dismissed as isolated issues early in the season has snowballed into one very lost and listless hockey team. Inconsistency, costly mistakes, and an inability to put together a complete 60-minute effort have fans wondering whether this team actually turned a corner last season — or if Buffalo simply rode the lightning of an incredible hot streak all the way back to the playoffs. Right now, the same old problems are rearing their ugly heads, joined by a few new ones that this team seems increasingly incapable of solving.



Key Issues Behind the Slow Start:




Inconsistent Goaltending and Defense: The Sabres rank near the bottom of the league in goals-against average, sitting 26th in the NHL, and have been hampered by inconsistent performances in net. Their numbers are even uglier at five-on-five, where they rank dead last at 32nd in the league. Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen has taken much of the heat, but pinning the blame solely on the goaltender is an easy way to ignore the bigger problem. Buffalo’s defense deserves its share of the criticism. Opponents are routinely left wide open in front of the net, the crease goes uncleared, and monumental breakdowns and costly turnovers continue to put Luukkonen in tough situations. No goaltender can consistently bail out a defense that makes life this difficult. Still, we’d all like to see an extra save or two from him each game. Neither is playing particularly well and that is a combo nobody wants.



Struggling Special Teams: The power play and penalty kill have been a continuous source of frustration for both fans and the media. Buffalo’s man advantage has been downright abysmal at times, showing little urgency and spending far too much time chasing the puck back into its own zone. When the Sabres finally manage to set up, they seem more interested in passing the puck around in search of the perfect shot than actually taking one. Inevitably, the opportunity goes up in smoke with a costly turnover, and the whole frustrating cycle starts all over again. The penalty kill has recently overtaken the power play as Buffalo’s biggest special-teams sore spot. The Sabres have surrendered a power-play goal in every game but one so far this season, and they currently sit 30th in the league with a miserable 66.7% success rate. Is there a word out there worse than abysmal? Whatever it is, it probably isn’t fit to print here.



Playing From Behind: Buffalo has repeatedly found itself chasing games early, and the constant need for comebacks is beginning to take its toll. Wednesday’s 3-1 loss to the Philadelphia Flyers showed that the Sabres don’t always have enough left in the tank to pull off another escape act. Before that game, Buffalo had trailed for a staggering 250:57, the fourth-highest total in the NHL. By comparison, the Sabres have held a lead for just 60:32 all season — barely the equivalent of one full game. Between the uneven goaltending, defensive breakdowns, and a laundry list of players failing to produce offensively, Buffalo is making life far harder than it needs to be. Considering how often this team has been forced to claw its way back from the brink of defeat, it’s a miracle the Sabres have managed to scrape together as many points as they have. That act is going to wear thin though. This team needs to put together a more consistent, 60-minute effort — something we have yet to see this season.



Offseason Regression Concerns: Buffalo had a difficult summer with roster turnover, and the early results have amplified worries about replicating last year’s success. Regression was expected from the national media right on down to our own fanbase. Nobody expected a repeat performance with the loss of Alex Tuch and Bowen Byram. A 4-4-2 record isn’t the end of the world, but at times, it sure feels that way. For much of the season, just about everything that could go wrong has gone wrong for Buffalo. Zach Benson and Peyton Krebs remain without a goal, while Ryan McLeod, Josh Doan, Konsta Helenius, and Jiri Kulich have managed just one goal apiece. Josh Norris has struggled as well, with only two goals and three points to his name. The defensive play and goaltending have been suspect, and the forwards haven’t exactly been helping matters with their backchecking. The Sabres continue to fall behind early and often, while the special teams have been downright awful. When performances are this consistently poor, questions about the coaching staff will arise too. It’s a perfect storm of dreadfulness, and Buffalo needs to right the ship before this disappointing start spirals further out of control.








Those are the main points of concern right now, but the list doesn’t end there. I haven’t even touched on Buffalo’s dreadful faceoff percentages and how those losses impact the rest of its game, from puck possession to controlling the pace of play. The Sabres also continue to lack physicality, and perhaps even more concerning, experience. After getting a little older last season, Buffalo has once again become the youngest team in the league. Youth brings plenty of talent and potential, but it also comes with growing pains. Right now, the Sabres are learning some hard lessons, and fans are left wondering how long it will take for this team to put all the pieces together. Or at least some of them.

Quick Thoughts



First Period – High-flying start to crash landing finish



The Sabres certainly looked like a team that came in with three days rest for much of the first period, but despite a number of golden chances and two power play opportunities, found themselves trailing by a pair of goals heading into the intermission.



Buffalo started the game with its two big returnees in Jason Zucker, who was making his season debut, and Rasmus Dahlin on the ice, and shortly after went to the power play due to a trip on Zach Benson. 



A Noah Ostlund between the legs attempt and passed up one-timer by Dahlin headlined what was a rare, chance-filled power play, but Flyers goalie Dan Vladar stonewalled the Sabres — a theme that continued throughout the period.



Not long after at 5-on-5, Mattias Samuelsson and Tage Thompson both had great looks from the slot, but the former’s shot was blocked and the latter was stifled by Vladar.



Philadelphia opened the scoring with just over five minutes remaining in the period, when a point shot by Oliver Bonk hit traffic in front and fell perfectly for Cole Knuble, who backhanded the puck over the outstretched pads of Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen. It was the first goal of Knuble’s NHL career, and scored with his dad Mike, a 16-year NHL veteran, in attendance.




Cole Knuble, 1-0 #LetsGoBuffalo #LetsGoFlyers pic.twitter.com/NDhGLQCQw9— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 22, 2026




The Sabres had a chance to even the score with another power play, but 40 seconds in, an Ostlund slashing penalty negated the man advantage. This gave Philadelphia a shortened power play of their own, and it wasn’t long before Buffalo’s penalty kill allowed yet another goal, as Trevor Zegras batted a rebound out of the air and into a wide open net to make it 2-0 with 43 seconds left in the period.



To make a bad final five minutes worse, a lackadaisical exchange between Owen Power and Jack Quinn sent Philadelphia’s Tyson Foerster in on a partial breakaway, and he was only stopped when an outstretched Quinn tripped him, giving the Flyers a near full power play to begin the second.



Despite tallying 10 high danger chances to the Flyers’ four, the Sabres found themselves in a familiar spot, down 2-0 heading to the intermission.



Second Period – Puck don’t lie



Benson got the second period off to a loud start, as he rung a shot off the post less than a minute in on a shorthanded chance. It wound up being the best opportunity for either team on the Flyers power play, as the Sabres successfully killed it off.



Once again, Buffalo controlled play at 5-on-5 for much of the period, and as a result had a number of great looks. Shortly after Philadelphia’s power play ended, Josh Doan ripped a shot from the high slot that required a flashy glove save from Vladar. Then it was the Sabres’ strongest line of Benson-Ostlund-Quinn who pinned the Flyers in their own zone, resulting in Quinn maneuvering his way to the slot and hitting Buffalo’s second post of the period.



A couple strong saves from Luukkonen kept the Sabres’ deficit at 2-0, before Zucker took a slashing penalty that sent Philadelphia back to the power play with just over five minutes to play. The Flyers would then get a 5-on-3 for just over a minute on an egregious call, as Zegras indirectly high sticked his teammate, Matvei Michkov, only for Power to be assessed the minor penalty. 



Despite the frustrating circumstances, the Sabres put together arguably their best penalty kill sequence of the young season, as Buffalo kept the Flyers off the board during both the 5-on-3 and ensuing power play thanks in-part to three shot blocks from Louis Crevier and some good saves from Luukkonen.



In what might best be described as a “puck don’t lie” sequence, the Sabres got a power play of their own less than a minute later when Benson drew his second penalty of the game, a high stick against Travis Sanheim. With 35 seconds left in the period, Quinn won a battle and found space along the wall to fire a puck at the net, which was deflected in on the doorstep by Zucker to finally beat Vladar and make it 2-1 heading to the third.




Jason Zucker, 2-1 PPG #LetsGoBuffalo #LetsGoFlyers pic.twitter.com/zjSW2t3DIK— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 22, 2026




Third Period – Ran out of gas 



Just when it seemed as if the Sabres had all the momentum, it was Knuble again who silenced KeyBank Center.



A failed clearing attempt resulted in the puck getting lost in the skates of Crevier. Bonk managed to gain control and find a streaking Knuble, who rounded Luukkonen and banked the puck back in off the retreating Sabres goalie. Luukkonen came out aggressively to challenge Knuble, which left him exposed at the post to add another questionable goal against to his shaky start of the season.




Knuble banks the puck off UPL from below the goal line and in. His 2nd of the game. 3-1 #LetsGoBuffalo #LetsGoFlyers pic.twitter.com/WeRSoCssTH— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) October 22, 2026




The Flyers’ third goal seemed to take the wind out of the Sabres’ sails, as they mustered just one shot on goal through the first 12 minutes of the period after controlling the game at 5-on-5 for a majority of the game prior. One of Buffalo’s only chances of the third period came from Benson with a wrist shot from the near faceoff dot, but he remained snakebitten in the offensive zone as Vladar came up with the save.



After Ryan McLeod was laid out on a clean hit by Hunter McDonald with about five minutes to play, Samuelsson stepped up and fought the Rochester native, earning himself an instigator penalty that gave the Flyers a power play and all but ended the game. 



Buffalo had one final opportunity with the goalie pulled, as Quinn took a one-timer with a gaping net in front of him, but Vladar had one more moment of magic in him as he pushed over to rob the 25-year-old and keep the score 3-1.



Quick Thoughts



The Sabres had numerous opportunities to take an early lead against a bad Flyers team, but failed to take them, resulting in yet another comeback attempt in hopes of securing a point. You can certainly say they got “goalie’d”, as Vladar was excellent and finished with 2.6 goals saved above expected, according to Hockeystats.com, but that does not excuse the lackluster third period.



Buffalo has still yet to put together a complete, dominant peformance so far this season, and tonight showed that thrilling third period comebacks are not a sustainable way to win. Additionally, they’ll need a lot more their stars, Dahlin and Thompson, going forward, as both were quiet throughout the game.




NHL Game Score Impact Card for Buffalo Sabres on 2026-10-21: pic.twitter.com/oLbi6bTYhj— HockeyStatCards (@hockeystatcards) October 22, 2026




Next Up



The Sabres begin a four-game road trip in Washington, with puck drop for 7 p.m. Saturday, before heading west to face the three California teams.

stories.title: Game #10 Preview & Open Thread: Buffalo Sabres vs Philadelphia Flyers
stories.summary:
Cavalry returns as Sabres host struggling Flyers



Buffalo Sabres (4-3-2) vs. Philadelphia Flyers (2-6-3)



Puck Drop: 7:30 p.m. ET | KeyBank Center, Buffalo, N.Y.



TV: TNT, TruTB, HBOMax



Radio: WGR 550, Sirius XM (app)



Know Your Opponent



Philadelphia Flyers



Record: 2-6-3 | 7 points



Last Game: 3-1 victory vs. Colorado



Division Ranking: 8th



PP: 27th, 4-31 (12.9%)  [Sabres: 32nd, 3-33 (9.09%)]



PK: 8th, 33-39 (84.6%) [Sabres: 30th, 20-31 (64.52%)]



Season Series: Sabres 2-1-0 vs. Flyers in 2025-26 season



What to watch



Triumphant Returns



Following last Saturday night’s overtime loss to the Montreal Canadiens, Buffalo Sabres head coach Lindy Ruff spoke with the media and gave encouraging updates on two players the Sabres have missed dearly.



Captain Rasmus Dahlin has not seen action since last Monday’s win against the Florida Panthers, where he left early in the second period with a lower body injury. Dahlin missed the ensuing three games for the Sabres, a stretch where they were able to go 1-0-2 without him in the lineup. While that record might not seem great, it is significantly better than how the team normally performs when Dahlin is out of the lineup, in that they actually were able to win one game. 



Thanks to this stretch of play where they were able to put up points in the standings, a stretch also headlined by fellow defensemen Owen Power, Mattias Samuelsson and Olen Zellweger stepping up in the captain’s stead, Dahlin was not forced to rush back to the lineup, giving him nearly 10 days to try and heal. While he is not guaranteed to be back in the lineup tonight, he spoke with the media after practice Monday and said it was his goal to be. The Sabres, especially given their defensive depth, should have it in their best interest to make sure Dahlin is healthy and at lower risk of reinjury, so if they have to hold him out another game or two, it shouldn’t be the end of the world.



There is one other player seemingly returning to the lineup though, as Ruff also said that tonight would be the target for winger Jason Zucker, who has not yet played a game this season due to offseason hernia surgery. 



The Sabres have missed Zucker quite a bit. He led the team in power play goals last season with 10 in just 62 games. He contributed 45 points in those 62 games as well, which is a nearly 60 point pace over a full season. 



While it is reasonable to temper expectations for a soon-to-be 35-year-old coming off hernia surgery, the Sabres have missed Zucker more than it may seem. The struggles of every forward line, other than the Quinn-Ostlund-Benson line, have been well documented, as no other group has garnered any consistent cohesion. This is partly due to a lot of guys who are normally center having to be moved to the wing. 



Adding an established, veteran winger to the mix could be exactly the piece the Sabres are missing in the short term, and Zucker provides even more than that. As the oldest player on the team, he provides a veteran leadership that can’t be matched by anyone else on the roster, and also provides a strong spark with his on-ice energy.



Fond Farewells? 



I would be remiss to sit here and ignore the Connor Hellebuyck-sized elephant (Helle-phant for short) in the room. All the buzz across the hockey world right now remains on the Winnipeg Jets goalie, and depending on what fake Twitter accounts you follow, he’s already been traded. With his suspension set to end this Friday, Jets GM Kevin Cheveldayoff could actually be forced to act on this situation that has been looming over his team, the Sabres, a handful of other teams, and the league as a whole since draft night in June.



With the potential impending threat of Hellebuyck reporting to camp, trade talks are fully back open and the Sabres are right in the thick of it, even viewed as the potential favorite depending on what part of twitter you’re reading. 



With that in mind, could Wednesday be the last game Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen plays in net for the Sabres? Could it be Ryan McLeod’s final game in blue and gold? What about Jiri Kulich? There are many rumors out there so be careful what you read, and of course the Sabres are not even guaranteed to land Hellebuyck, but there is a real, potentially very real scenario, that at least two of the aforementioned players, if not all three, are not on the Sabres after tonight’s game. We’ll just have to wait and see.



The Philadelphia Grounders



We’re this far in and the Sabres opponent has barely been mentioned so far. If you haven’t been keeping up, the Flyers are off to just about the worst start to a season a team can have. While they are currently riding a two game winning streak, with victories over the Ottawa Senators and Colorado Avalanche, those represent their first two wins of the season, coming in games 10 and 11. 



Head coach Rick Tocchet is under serious heat for how the season has started, and not just for how the team is playing. One of the most notorious headlines to start this season has been how Tocchet and the Flyers have treated young forwards Matvei Michkov and Porter Martone. 



Despite leading the team in goals and points, with six and seven respectively, Michkov is playing just under 15 minutes per game, while Martone is getting even less, at 13:15 per game. This puts them at seventh and 10th on the team so far among forwards, and for a team that is struggling as heavily as they are, you’d think they’d be incentivized to give the young, promising players a bit more run, but Tocchet has taken the opposite approach. 



One bright spot for the Flyers, however, has been in net, particularly with Joseph Woll. Woll, who came over from the Toronto Maple Leafs in the offseason, has been stellar for the Flyers, putting up a .916 save% in five games played to start the year.



Injury Updates



While the Sabres are likely getting two players returning to the lineup, they are also evaluating a couple guys for injuries. With the forward depth they currently have, it is not a dire straits situation, but both Justin Danforth and Sam Carrick are being evaluated for injuries. Both of these injuries are listed as upper-body and both are considered day to day. Carrick’s injury is potentially related to the injury he suffered at the end of last season. 



Connor Timmins, still out with a lower-body injury, is not yet ready to return to full practice and Alex Lyon is “improving” according to Lindy Ruff, but has not rejoined the team on the ice. Lyon suffered a setback in his recovery last week.

Excitement!



DBTB –



Let me be honest:  I am getting excited about this Class.  There you go.  Now you know.  Will the Sabres have a 1st round pick this year?  Will they wind up with more than one?  Who can say?  Nobody at this time last year thought they would be selecting at #4 overall AND #20, but that’s exactly what happened.  So strange things can occur.  Thus, I will continue to follow these young prospects, really more for my own entertainment, but also for you, DBTB, in the event you have a hankering for some junior hockey or are, like Casey Kasem before you, keeping your feet on the ground while reaching for (future) stars! 



Why, McGee?  What makes you like this year’s class?  Let’s get into it.  First off, I think drafts are largely valued by how many first-line centers might be in the class.  Some of the great drafts – 1979, 1984, 2003, 2015 – have been anchored by superstar centers.  Lemieux, McDavid, Eichel, Aho, Getzlaf, Staal, Bergeron, etc.  This Draft class has some potential high-end #1 centers – Milan Sundstrom, Yevgeni Yakunin, Alexis Joseph, Jonah Neuenschwander, Brock England, Jaakko Wycisk, Carter Meyer, Max Calce.  Some of those, maybe all of them, will not pan out as 1Cs, but there’s a chance several of them could.  That would automatically make this Draft memorable.  Another thing those elite drafts had were top end D-Men.  2003 had Shea Weber and Ryan Suter.  2015 had Zach Werenski.  1979 had Ray Bourque and Kevin Lowe.  This draft has Landon Dupont, right now the consensus #1 overall.  Assuming he lives up to the hype, that’s another point in this Draft’s favor.  Lastly, an assortment of high-powered offensive forwards is a must.  Marner, Rantanen, and Connor came out of the 2015 class.  1984 had Gary Roberts, Brett Hull, and Luc Robitaille.  Back in 2003, they had Pavelski, Corey Perry, Thomas Vanek, Jeff Carter, Parise, and Brett Burns (some of you will know that Burns was drafted as a right wing and played win in the NHL when he broke in before they switched him to defense).  This year’s Draft has 3 Russian forwards: Privalov, Skvortsov, and Pustovoy.  It also has Dima Zhilkin, Tomas Selic, Tim Kazda, and Noah Davidson, among others.  All of them could be super-productive top-line players.   



Now, just to be clear, I’m not saying this is guaranteed to be an all-time Draft.  Just that it has the potential to receive such lofty status.  What’s the hold up, you might ask.



At the moment, we’re still in the infancy of the 2027 Draft year.  Some teams over in Europe or Russia have played 8-10 games, but most are below that.  Here in North America, at the time of this typing the CHL is only a couple games into the season, while the USHL has barely gotten underway and the NCAA will kick off this weekend. 



What about the Sabres, you might say.  Isn’t this a Sabres’ site?  Indeed it is.  The BFLO prospect pool hasn’t played much as of yet, as they are heavily into the NCAA which just got underway.  But some standouts are worth mentioning here.  First off, Jake Richard.  The big-shot forward and AHL rookie has looked really good, contributing 2P in 2 games in the pre-season, and added his first goal in Game 1 of the Amerks’ season.  If he continues to put up points, he will have exceeded a lot of expectations.  In Russia, Prokhor Poltapov has 5P in 11 games on the best team in the league, loaded with former NHLers and former draft picks.   In the Quebec League, Samuel Meloche has been one of the league’s best goaltenders, notching a 2.54 GAA and a .913 SV% between the pipes for Saint John.  More to come of course, but the Sabres pipeline still looks impressive.



For the last time this season, I’ll be using the odds from the sportsbook at the Wynn in Las Vegas, and then running them through the Tankathon simulator to get my drafting order.  When we hit the November Mock Draft, we’ll have some actual standings that will determine the order of selection.  Until then, we’ll stick with this!

Sabres Analysis



1#20: BUFFALO: Luca Santala, 6’3 C/RW, OHL:  



This Finnish kid might be a little too similar to Ilya Morozov, but you can never have too many good two-way centermen.  Santala has great size (6’2 195#), and the best word I’ve seen used to describe him is ‘complete’.  He can play up and down the line-up, has a mature defensive game even at his young age, and is dangerous on specials teams.  Versatility is another way to describe his game.  A natural goal-scorer, Santala seems like he’s always ready to shoot.  Stick on the ice, feet positioned correctly, has a quick, deadly release whether off the pass, pouncing on a loose puck, or carrying it himself.  Accurate, hard wrister which he can get off without a moment’s hesitation.  Superb hands.  Really good on tips, deflections, and quick shots in tight.  Strong on his skates.  Can power through stick checks with or without the puck.  Real nose for the puck.  Is a clever playmaker, sees the ice well, especially in transition.  



While he seems to be more of a shooter than a passer, he makes the right decisions with the puck in the offensive zone and creates time and space with his puck handling to open things up for teammates.  Slippery with or without the puck, has the courage to try a lot of different things and often gets away with them.  Strong skater, but still room to improve.  His straight-line speed is good, and he’s elusive with the puck, but his motor sometimes seems to downshift for stretches in-game.  That needs to improve, but it’s not that unusual for a number of Finnish prospects…for example, Anton Lundell used to have that same criticism of his game around the same age.  



Defensively, Santala has really good instincts.  On the puck, he uses a quick stick and his smarts to close out his check and take the puck away.  In space, he can flash some high-level defensive recognition, but like his motor, sometimes that wanes for periods during the game.  Could stand to play a little deeper in his own end, especially when playing center.  Santala has the ability to be a valuable #2 center, or he can play wing and serve as a one-timer threat on the PP.  Was great in the Hlinka tournament with 6P in 5 games for the Finns.  Came over to North American this year, intending to play for Dale Hunter and the London Knights, but was traded almost immediately to the Kitchener Rangers (due to some rules re: import players in CHL) where he’ll get plenty of opportunities to play.  Could be a bigger, stronger Mikel Granlund when all is said and done.  And there’s something to be said for that. 













2#20: BUFFALO: Ben Nystrom, 6’3 C/W, SWE:  



A monster on skates, Nystrom is an often-overlooked player out of Sweden.  At 6’3 200#, he’s got plenty of size, and the flexibility to play center or wing.  He’s also a physical presence who has shown a surprising aptitude for scoring.  Make no mistake, Nystrom is a big body who loves to mix it up.  A puck possession beast, knows how to use his size to shield the puck from opponents while looking for open teammates.  Wins more than his share of board battles.  Fearless in going to the corners or behind the net to dig out pucks.  That fearlessness comes from using his obvious size advantage, including his length, to take on smaller players and just overpower them.  But this kid is not a one-trick pony.  He understands how to use that advantage to improve other parts of his game.  



Surprisingly good hands allow him to handle the puck while protecting it and lets him see the ice well enough to make plays and distribute the puck with some skill.  In particular, he can be dangerous out of the cycle, going low to high or cross-crease to set up teammates when he comes out of the corners with the puck, which he does the majority of the time.  Also owns a quick, heavy and dangerous wrister, that he can get off in close quarters with velocity.  Could use some more variety in his shot arsenal, but he’s not a goal-scorer from distance so that might not be as big of a deal.  Encourages a physical game.  Will run opponents over to recover pucks or blast his check with a heavy hit into the boards.  Also tough to handle around the crease, where he uses his length and power to set up shop and can’t be moved.  



Defensively willing, an eager back-checker.  Loves to separate an opponent from the puck and is a very dangerous forechecker with a great sense of timing to jump a passing lane or just take the body and force a turnover.  Has had a great start in the U20 Swedish league with 6P in 7 games.  Was such a productive player at the Hlinka tournament last Spring, he played the final games on the top line for Team Sweden.  Has a lot of similar qualities to former Sabre prospect Anton Wahlberg, but with more of a physical edge.  Reminds me a bit of long-time NHL’er David Backes. 







3#15: BUFFALO (WASHINGTON/SAN JOSE):  Bogdan Yakushevsky, 6’0 W, OHL:  



With a name like a hardware store owner from Cheektowaga, you might be fooled into thinking you know what kind of player he is.  But it’s very likely he goes higher than this from what I’ve seen.  Let’s hope he slides to BFLO.  This kid is a dogged, relentless forward with a ton of skill.  A dynamic puck handler and playmaker, he’s equal parts scorer and passer which makes him all the more difficult to stop.  A player with a great burst, he can get out of the gates in a flash and explodes down the ice.  Couple that with his handle and he makes a lot happen with the puck on his stick in transition.  Takes unexpected routes to the net.  Agility is very good, allows him to go inside or out with ease and keep defenders off guard.  



An absolute terror in puck pursuit.  Yakushevsky never quits on a puck, even when it is recovered by another team.  He’s fast and physical, even at 6’0 190#.  Will throw some big checks on the forecheck, but he gets inside opponents, ties up their hands, and forces turnovers.  Like Zach Benson, he’s always F1 on the forecheck.  Comes barreling in without a second of hesitation.  If he misses the opponent, he’s instantly after them like a dog on a bone.  His unceasing motor has him going all out seemingly every shift.  Puck pursuit is top notch.  But what makes him especially valuable is his ability to score.  Armed with a rocket shot, elusiveness, and the ability to create time and space for himself, he’s a threat all over the ice.  Deceptive with his shot, he can disguise it with a series of fakes or use a defender to hide his intentions until he rips a shot.  And that shot is precise and heavy, enabling him to score from the top of the circles on down, often beating goalies clean from distance.  



A true competitor, the kind the Sabres have been drafting of late (Benson, Helenius, Morozov, Ziemer, etc), he fits a need and a pattern for Jerry Forton and his team.  Unexpectedly came over to North America this year, signing with the Windsor Spitfires and taking the CHL by storm with 5P in 4 games already.  If I squint hard enough, I can see a Sam Bennett-type of player here.   







3#20: BUFFALO: Grady Pichette, 6’4 RHD, WHL:  



Another quality name, the Sabres have made a living the last few years drafting big, rangy defensemen who can skate and play both ways.  In this scenario, they find another one at the back-end of the 3rd round.  Pichette meets all the criteria.  Skating is smooth and effortless for a kid of his size.  He can explode up ice or use his tight turns to recover when transition goes bad and he needs to protect his own end.  When forced to defend he uses that smooth skating and his length to close off opponents and eliminate their options.  Difficult to get behind him.  Meticulous in his play, he has a knack for doing the little things – angling forwards off to the perimeter, maintaining stick-on-puck, tying guys up around the net – that will help him as he continues to evolve.  Really came on in the back-half of last season, when things seemed to click for him.  



Truly more of a puck transporter than an offensive or shut-down guy, he has some upside on both ends.  Needs to play more physical in his D-zone.  Pairing that up with his skating and length would make him an effective shut-down guy not unlike a bigger Ryan Johnson.  Getting more confidence on the offensive side of the puck should allow him to trigger transition more efficiently and then trail the play or even lead the rush more often and create chances from the back-end.  Has all the physical tools the Sabres look for, now he just needs some coaching to start building out his game.  



Playing on an improving Lethbridge team should help with that.  He’s their best defender in the early going this year.  Could become a Marcus Pettersson-type of defender, which has a lot of value in the NHL these days.
